label: Verve
rationale: At the Montreux Jazz Festival is the live record of Bill Evans's late-1960s trio — Eddie Gómez on bass, Jack DeJohnette on drums — and the one that won the 1969 Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album, Individual or Group [S1] (obs). Consensus across independent traditions of listing: Wikipedia's review box records AllMusic at four stars and The Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings at three and a half [S1] (obs), and AllMusic files it under Post-Bop, Modal Music and Piano Jazz while rating it four stars [S2] (obs). Defining statement: AllMusic's review calls it 'the beginning of stylistic changes for the legendary pianist', 'more lively, playful, and experimental' than At Town Hall and 'his most extroverted playing since his freshman release, New Jazz Conceptions' [S1,S2] (obs) — i.e. the record where the introspective 1961 trio gives way to the harder-swinging Gómez/DeJohnette band. Lineage: 'Nardis', the Miles Davis tune Evans never cut in a Verve studio, is here in its defining live reading, and the performance was later sampled by MF Doom on 'Raid' from Madvillainy — influence audible well outside jazz [S1] (obs); the album is the fourth Evans record the canon needs to hold the arc the three Village Vanguard records and Portrait in Jazz begin [S1,S2] (inf). It still plays: a festival audience, a long 'Nardis', 'A Sleepin' Bee', 'Embraceable You', 'Some Day My Prince Will Come' — the trio at its most outgoing [S1,S2] (obs). Boundary note: 1968, comfortably inside the window; post-bop/modal, no scope question — the council's tier is the only open question.

personnel_record.notes: Single session: the trio's June 15, 1968 set at the Montreux Jazz Festival, in the Casino de Montreux — the original 1881 building, three years before the 1971 fire that closed it. The original Verve LP (V6-8762) carries the nine tracks listed above; CD and later editions add a spoken introduction and 'Quiet Now' (Denny Zeitlin), which is why Wikipedia's track table runs to eleven items and AllMusic gives the album as 58:59 while the LP timings sum to roughly 47 minutes [S1,S2,S3]. Only the nine original LP tracks are recorded here. The Apple Music edition found by the iTunes lookup (collectionId 1425178671) is the 10-track digital release [S5]. Production detail is unusually well documented for a live date: producer Helen Keane; recorded by the technical department of Radio Suisse Romande, with sound engineers Pierre Grandjean and Jean-Claude Martin, editing/remix engineer Bob Schwarz, engineering director Val Valentin and art direction by Acy R. Lehman [S3,S4]. Track-title variants: the LP label prints 'A Sleeping Bee' and 'Someday My Prince Will Come'; the standard song forms are used here, with the personnel 'tracks' arrays matching on the standard forms. The album is titled 'Bill Evans at the Montreux Jazz Festival' on Wikipedia and MusicBrainz and 'At the Montreux Jazz Festival' on the AllMusic, Discogs and Apple releases; the release title is used as the album name.

ballot.album: Bill Evans — At the Montreux Jazz Festival (1968)
ballot.case_for: The 1969 Grammy, AllMusic’s four-star rating, and Penguin Guide’s 3.5-star rating provide meaningful recognition, while AllMusic describes the set as the beginning of stylistic changes for Evans. The Gómez–DeJohnette trio offers a distinct, more extroverted chapter beyond the celebrated LaFaro–Motian Vanguard recordings; its live “Nardis” and the album’s festival energy make it both a valuable career document and an inviting listen (S1, S2).
ballot.case_against: The critical-consensus case rests mainly on two ratings and a Grammy; the dossier’s other sources largely establish metadata rather than independent critical standing. Even as a distinctive second-trio document, it may strengthen an Evans arc already represented by the Vanguard records and Portrait in Jazz more than fill an unmistakable gap.
ballot.recommendation: John should treat this as a strong-priority consensus-core candidate, while reserving the inclusion decision for himself.
